case: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of high blood pressure found at a pre-employment examination. Between ages 2 and 7 years, she had repeated febrile urinary tract infections. She takes no medications. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Urinalysis shows 2+ protein with negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Ultrasonography shows a small left kidney (8.2 cm) with coarse, irregular cortical scars overlying dilated, blunted calyces; the right kidney measures 12.0 cm and appears normal. Diagnosis: chronic pyelonephritis due to reflux nephropathy.

questions.stem: Records show that cystoscopy at age 5 years found the left ureteral orifice displaced laterally on the bladder base, with a short submucosal ureteral tunnel. Which of the following developmental events most likely produced this orifice position?
options: Persistent obstruction of the ureteric lumen during fetal recanalization
Origin of the ureteric bud at an abnormally caudal site on the mesonephric duct
Origin of the ureteric bud at an abnormally cranial site on the mesonephric duct
Early division of the ureteric bud into two separate branches
approach: Link the finding to the problem: a lateral orifice with a short tunnel is the classic setup for reflux.
Recall how the orifice gets its position: the caudal mesonephric duct is absorbed into the bladder wall, and the ureteric orifice then migrates cranially and laterally.
A bud that starts too low is absorbed early and migrates too far, so it ends up lateral with a short tunnel.
questions.why: The ureteric bud grows out of the mesonephric duct just above where the duct enters the urogenital sinus, the future bladder. As the end of the mesonephric duct is absorbed into the bladder wall, the ureteric orifice moves cranially and laterally. A bud that arises too caudally is absorbed early and travels too far, so its orifice sits lateral on the bladder base with a short intravesical segment. A short tunnel is not squeezed shut when the bladder contracts, so urine refluxes up the ureter.
whyNot: Incomplete recanalization of the ureter has been proposed as a cause of congenital ureteral narrowing, such as ureteropelvic junction obstruction. It narrows the lumen and does not move the orifice laterally.
Correct.

A bud that arises too cranially is absorbed late and stays caudal and medial, so its orifice lands near the bladder neck or in the urethra. That ectopic position tends to cause obstruction, or continuous dribbling in girls when the orifice lies below the sphincter.
Early splitting of a single bud gives a bifid ureter that joins before the bladder and drains through one orifice in a normal position.

topics: Ureteric bud origin and orifice position

questions.stem: Her reflux was never documented during childhood. Which of the following studies would have most directly demonstrated the abnormality that led to her renal scarring?
options: Renal ultrasonography with Doppler flow
Technetium-99m DMSA cortical scan
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT
Voiding cystourethrography
approach: Name the underlying problem: childhood febrile infections plus scarring over blunted calyces point to vesicoureteral reflux.
Ask what reflux requires to be seen: contrast inside the bladder, imaged while the bladder contracts.
Only a voiding cystourethrogram fills the bladder with contrast and watches it move up the ureter during voiding.
questions.why: Primary vesicoureteral reflux comes from a short intravesical ureteral segment. Normally the ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall, so rising bladder pressure during voiding flattens it like a flap valve. When the segment is short, the valve fails and urine is pushed up toward the kidney, carrying bacteria with it. A voiding cystourethrogram fills the bladder with contrast through a catheter and images the patient while voiding, so it shows the reflux itself and its grade.
whyNot: Ultrasonography shows kidney size, scars, and hydronephrosis, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude reflux because it does not image urine moving backward during voiding.
A DMSA scan shows cortical scars and acute pyelonephritis. It documents the damage, not the reflux that caused it.
CT shows renal scarring and complications such as abscess. It exposes a child to radiation and does not image the bladder during voiding.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her blood pressure remains elevated even though her daily sodium excretion matches her sodium intake and her plasma volume is stable. Which of the following best explains how her scarred kidney sustains the hypertension?
options: A higher arterial pressure is needed to excrete her daily sodium load
Excess aldosterone secretion that does not depend on renin release
Sustained rise in cardiac output from a continually expanding plasma volume
Resetting of carotid sinus baroreceptors to a higher pressure
approach: Note that she is in sodium balance: output equals intake and volume is steady.
Recall pressure natriuresis: the kidney excretes more sodium as arterial pressure rises, and long-term pressure settles where output equals intake.
Apply it: a scarred kidney with fewer working nephrons reaches that balance only at a higher pressure.
questions.why: Pressure natriuresis is the kidney's long-term control of blood pressure. When arterial pressure rises, the kidney excretes more sodium and water, which lowers volume and brings pressure back down. Over weeks, arterial pressure settles at the point where sodium output equals intake. Scarring with nephron loss, and renin release from ischemic areas, shift this pressure natriuresis curve to the right, so balance is reached only at a higher arterial pressure.
whyNot: Correct.
Primary hyperaldosteronism raises pressure with low renin and hypokalemia. Nothing here suggests an adrenal source, and renal scarring tends to raise renin rather than suppress it.
Her plasma volume is stable, so volume is not still expanding. Once balance is restored, the hypertension is maintained by the kidney's higher set point.
Baroreceptors reset to a new pressure within days. They buffer short-term changes and cannot set the long-term level of arterial pressure.

questions.stem: Her kidney function continues to decline, and the left kidney is eventually removed. Microscopic examination of the scarred regions is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Fibrocellular crescents filling Bowman space
Concentric onion-skin thickening of arteriolar walls
Atrophic tubules filled with eosinophilic hyaline casts
Patchy tubular necrosis with muddy brown granular casts
approach: Identify the lesion: chronic pyelonephritis from reflux, with scars over blunted calyces.
Recall its microscopy: chronic interstitial inflammation, interstitial fibrosis, and atrophic, dilated tubules.
Pick the classic picture: tubules packed with pink casts that look like thyroid follicles (thyroidization).
questions.why: Chronic pyelonephritis is a tubulointerstitial disease. Scarred areas show interstitial fibrosis, lymphocytes and plasma cells, and atrophic tubules that are dilated and filled with eosinophilic hyaline casts. Rows of these tubules look like thyroid follicles, so the pattern is called thyroidization. Glomeruli are spared early, though some later develop periglomerular fibrosis and secondary segmental sclerosis, which explains her proteinuria.
whyNot: Crescents form in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis when fibrin and cells fill Bowman space. Reflux nephropathy damages tubules and interstitium first.
Onion-skin arteriolar thickening is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis from malignant hypertension. Her hypertension is moderate and secondary to the scarring.
Correct.
Muddy brown casts and patchy tubular necrosis are the signs of acute tubular necrosis, an acute injury. Her disease is chronic and scarring.

dx: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis with an obstructing stone
case: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of dull right flank pain, intermittent low-grade fever, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL (12 to 16), and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Urine pH is 8.5 (4.5 to 8.0), and urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis. CT shows an enlarged, poorly functioning right kidney with a branching staghorn calculus filling the renal pelvis and calyces, and dilated calyces surrounded by low-density masses. The left kidney is normal. Right nephrectomy is performed. Diagnosis: xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis with an obstructing staghorn calculus.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties of the infecting organism most directly explains the composition of her calculus?
options: Nitrate reductase activity that generates urinary nitrite
Lactose fermentation that produces organic acids in urine
Urease activity that splits urea into ammonia
Swarming motility that spreads it along the urothelium
approach: Connect the clues: Proteus, alkaline urine, and a staghorn calculus.
Recall that staghorn stones in infected, alkaline urine are struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate).
Ask what makes urine alkaline and supplies ammonium: urease splitting urea.
questions.why: Proteus mirabilis makes urease, which splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Ammonia takes up hydrogen ions to form ammonium, and the urine pH rises above about 7. In alkaline urine, magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate precipitate as struvite, often mixed with calcium phosphate. These stones grow quickly into a staghorn shape and shelter bacteria, which keeps the infection going.
whyNot: Nitrate reductase gives a positive nitrite dipstick in Enterobacterales infections. Nitrite does not change urine pH or form stones.
Proteus does not ferment lactose. Acid production would lower urine pH, which favors uric acid stones rather than struvite.
Correct.
Swarming motility is a laboratory clue, a spreading film of growth on agar plates. It helps identify Proteus but has no role in stone chemistry.

questions.stem: Preoperative imaging raised concern for renal cell carcinoma. The cut surface of the resected kidney shows yellow-orange nodules surrounding the dilated calyces. Microscopic examination of these nodules is most likely to show sheets of which of the following?
options: Lipid-laden foamy macrophages
Polygonal clear cells in nests with delicate vessels
Epithelioid histiocytes in caseating granulomas
Neutrophils within tubules and the interstitium
approach: Identify the setting: a chronic obstructed infection with Proteus and a staghorn stone.
Recall the host response in xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis: macrophages take up lipid from destroyed tissue and fail to clear the bacteria.
Yellow nodules made of foamy macrophages explain why it can look like a clear cell tumor.
questions.why: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a chronic destructive infection, usually behind an obstructing stone and often with Proteus or E. coli. Macrophages flood the kidney, ingest lipid released from damaged tissue, and become foamy. Mixed with plasma cells, lymphocytes, and giant cells, they form yellow nodules that replace the parenchyma. On imaging and grossly this can mimic renal cell carcinoma, and the foamy macrophages can resemble tumor clear cells under the microscope.
whyNot: Correct.

Nests of clear epithelial cells with a fine vascular network describe clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the lesion this condition mimics. The infection and staghorn stone favor xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.
Caseating granulomas suggest renal tuberculosis, which gives sterile pyuria on routine culture. Her culture grew Proteus.
Neutrophils in tubules and interstitium are the picture of acute pyelonephritis. Her months-long destructive process with yellow nodules is chronic.

questions.stem: CT also shows that the inflammation has spread through the anterior surface of the medial part of the right kidney, near the hilum, and formed a fistula into adjacent bowel. Which of the following structures is most likely involved?
options: Right colic flexure
Horizontal part of the duodenum
Right lobe of the liver
Descending part of the duodenum
approach: Locate the leak: anterior, medial, at the level of the hilum of the right kidney.
List the anterior relations of the right kidney: liver above, right colic flexure at the lower lateral part, and the descending duodenum medially.
The only bowel lying on the medial, hilar part is the descending (second) part of the duodenum.
questions.why: The front of the right kidney touches three main structures. The right lobe of the liver covers the upper part, separated by the hepatorenal recess. The right colic flexure lies on the lower lateral part. The descending part of the duodenum lies on the medial part near the hilum. Inflammation breaking through the anteromedial surface at the hilum would therefore reach the descending duodenum, and renoduodenal fistulas are a recognized complication of this infection.
whyNot: The right colic flexure lies against the lower lateral part of the right kidney. A fistula from that region would enter the colon.
The horizontal part of the duodenum crosses the midline at about L3, below the kidney and in front of the inferior vena cava and aorta. It does not lie on the renal hilum.
The liver lies in front of the upper part of the right kidney and is not bowel. Spread there would form a hepatic abscess.
Correct.

questions.stem: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, which this lesion resembled, can raise the hematocrit by producing erythropoietin. In a normal kidney, which of the following best describes how erythropoietin production is regulated?
options: Low perfusion pressure triggers its release from juxtaglomerular cells
Hypoxia stabilizes HIF in peritubular interstitial fibroblasts
Hypoxia increases HIF hydroxylation in proximal tubule cells
High tubular sodium chloride signals the macula densa to release it
approach: Name the stimulus: low oxygen delivery to the kidney, not low pressure or salt.
Recall the molecular switch: with normal oxygen, HIF-alpha is hydroxylated and destroyed; with hypoxia, it survives and turns on the erythropoietin gene.
Place it in the right cells: fibroblast-like interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries.
questions.why: Erythropoietin is made by fibroblast-like interstitial cells next to the peritubular capillaries of the cortex and outer medulla. With normal oxygen, prolyl hydroxylases use oxygen to hydroxylate HIF-alpha, and the VHL protein tags it for destruction. In hypoxia, hydroxylation stops, HIF-alpha builds up, and it switches on the erythropoietin gene. Clear cell carcinoma usually loses VHL, so HIF stays active and can drive erythropoietin release and polycythemia. Loss of these interstitial cells in chronic kidney disease causes normocytic anemia, while her own anemia reflects chronic inflammation because her left kidney is normal.
whyNot: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin when afferent arteriolar pressure falls. They do not make erythropoietin.
Correct.
HIF hydroxylation happens when oxygen is plentiful and leads to HIF breakdown. Hypoxia stops hydroxylation, and the producing cells are interstitial cells rather than tubular epithelium.
The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone and renin release. It does not release erythropoietin.

case: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 18-month history of suprapubic pain that worsens as her bladder fills and eases after voiding. She urinates about 16 times daily and twice nightly and has a near-constant urge to void. Five urine cultures obtained during symptomatic periods showed no growth, and several courses of antibiotics did not help. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows suprapubic and anterior vaginal wall tenderness. Urine cytology is negative. Cystoscopy with hydrodistention shows pinpoint submucosal hemorrhages and a reddened mucosal patch with radiating vessels on the bladder dome. Diagnosis: interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome) with a Hunner lesion.

questions.stem: At her first visit, she was treated for presumed bacterial cystitis. Which of the following urine dipstick results would most specifically have indicated infection with Escherichia coli or another member of the Enterobacterales?
options: Positive nitrite
Positive leukocyte esterase
Positive blood
Elevated specific gravity
approach: Ask what each dipstick pad detects: white cells, red cells, concentration, or a bacterial product.
Recall that Enterobacterales carry nitrate reductase, which turns dietary nitrate in urine into nitrite.
Only the nitrite pad detects a product made by the bacteria themselves.
questions.why: Gram-negative enteric rods such as E. coli, Klebsiella, and Proteus reduce urinary nitrate to nitrite with nitrate reductase. A positive nitrite test therefore points to these organisms specifically. The test needs a few hours of bladder dwell time, so frequent voiding, as in this patient, can cause false negatives. Enterococci and Staphylococcus saprophyticus usually give a negative nitrite test.
whyNot: Correct.
Leukocyte esterase detects neutrophils, so it shows pyuria from any cause. Sterile pyuria occurs in urethritis from Chlamydia and in renal tuberculosis.
A positive blood pad detects hemoglobin or myoglobin. It occurs with stones, tumors, glomerular disease, and inflamed mucosa, so it does not point to a bacterial cause.
Specific gravity reflects urine concentration and hydration. It says nothing about infection.

questions.stem: She also reports leaking small amounts of urine when she coughs, sneezes, or lifts her children, with no preceding urge. She has had three vaginal deliveries. Which of the following best explains this leakage?
options: Involuntary detrusor contractions during bladder filling
Bladder overdistension from impaired detrusor contraction
Weakened pelvic floor support of the proximal urethra
Fistula between the bladder and the anterior vagina
approach: Classify the leak: small volumes with coughing or lifting and no urge is stress incontinence.
Recall what normally prevents it: the levator ani and endopelvic fascia hold the proximal urethra so abdominal pressure compresses it as much as the bladder.
Vaginal deliveries can weaken that support, so the urethra drops and opens under strain.
questions.why: Normally the bladder neck and proximal urethra sit on a hammock of levator ani and endopelvic fascia. When abdominal pressure rises, it squeezes the urethra as well as the bladder, so the urethra stays closed. Stretching or tearing of this support during vaginal delivery lets the urethra become hypermobile and drop below it. Then a cough raises bladder pressure above urethral closing pressure, and urine leaks without any detrusor contraction.
whyNot: Involuntary detrusor contractions cause urge incontinence, with a sudden strong need to void before leakage. Her leakage has no urge.
Poor detrusor contraction leads to retention and overflow incontinence, with constant dribbling from an overfull bladder, as in diabetic neuropathy or outlet obstruction.
Correct.
A vesicovaginal fistula causes continuous leakage from the vagina regardless of effort. It typically follows pelvic surgery, radiation, or obstructed labor.

topics: Pelvic floor support of the urethra

questions.stem: One proposed mechanism of her disorder is a defect in the bladder lining that lets urinary solutes, such as potassium, reach suburothelial nerves. During normal bladder filling, which of the following allows the lining to stretch while staying impermeable?
options: Tight junctions between surface cells open to relieve tension
Umbrella cells flatten and insert stored membrane vesicles
Keratinized squamous surface cells slide over each other
Intermediate cells divide rapidly to cover the larger surface
approach: Identify the tissue: urothelium (transitional epithelium) with large surface umbrella cells.
Recall the barrier: umbrella cells have tight junctions and an apical membrane of stiff uroplakin plaques.
Recall how it stretches: the cells flatten, and stored vesicles fuse with the apical membrane to add surface area without opening any gaps.
questions.why: The urothelium lines the bladder with several layers of cells topped by large umbrella cells. Their apical membrane is built of rigid uroplakin plaques sealed by tight junctions, which makes a strong barrier to urine. As the bladder fills, the umbrella cells flatten and fuse stored membrane vesicles into their apical surface, so the lining enlarges while the barrier stays intact. When the bladder empties, the extra membrane is taken back in. Damage to this barrier is one theory for the pain of interstitial cystitis.
whyNot: Opening tight junctions would let urine leak into the bladder wall. The junctions stay sealed during filling.
Correct.
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers skin. The bladder has a nonkeratinized transitional epithelium.
Bladder filling happens over minutes to hours, far too fast for cell division. The lining enlarges by changing cell shape and adding membrane.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the reddened patch is taken to exclude carcinoma in situ. Which of the following microscopic findings is most consistent with her diagnosis?
options: Full-thickness urothelial atypia with loss of polarity
Sheets of macrophages containing Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
Nests of urothelium in the lamina propria with central lumens
Mucosal ulceration with chronic inflammation and mast cells
approach: Recall that interstitial cystitis is a diagnosis of exclusion: cultures are negative and cytology rules out tumor.
Recall the Hunner lesion: a reddened area of mucosa with radiating vessels that may ulcerate.
Match the histology: ulceration with chronic inflammation and fibrosis through the wall, with prominent mast cells.
questions.why: Interstitial cystitis is chronic bladder pain with urgency and frequency in the absence of infection, and it is much more common in women. Some patients have Hunner lesions, patches of reddened mucosa that ulcerate. Biopsy shows mucosal ulceration, chronic inflammation, and fibrosis that can extend through the wall, and mast cells are characteristically increased. The biopsy matters because carcinoma in situ of the bladder can cause the same urgency and frequency.
whyNot: Full-thickness atypia with loss of polarity is urothelial carcinoma in situ, the lesion this biopsy is meant to exclude. Her cytology was negative.
Macrophages with laminated Michaelis-Gutmann bodies define malakoplakia, a reaction to chronic bacterial infection, usually E. coli. Her cultures are sterile.
Nests of urothelium with central lumens are cystitis cystica, a common reactive change. It does not cause the chronic pain syndrome described.
Correct.

dx: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with a ruptured berry aneurysm
case: A 44-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of a severe headache that he describes as the worst of his life. He has a 6-year history of hypertension and has had two episodes of flank pain with gross hematuria. His father began dialysis at age 52 years. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 182/104 mm Hg. He has nuchal rigidity. Large, nodular masses are palpable in both flanks. Serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Noncontrast CT of the head shows blood in the basal cisterns. Abdominal CT shows bilaterally enlarged kidneys replaced by numerous cysts. Diagnosis: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

questions.stem: His sister's newborn son has a palpable left flank mass. Ultrasonography shows a left kidney replaced by noncommunicating cysts of varying size with no recognizable normal parenchyma. The right kidney and amniotic fluid volume were normal. Which of the following best describes the infant's condition?
options: An early presentation of his uncle's inherited disease
Autosomal recessive cystic disease with hepatic fibrosis
Acquired cysts from dilated tubules after tubular injury
A sporadic malformation of metanephric differentiation
approach: Note the pattern: one kidney replaced by cysts of varying size, with a normal opposite kidney and normal amniotic fluid.
Compare cystic diseases: polycystic disease of either inheritance pattern involves both kidneys, and acquired cystic disease follows years of dialysis.
A unilateral cystic, nonfunctioning kidney in a newborn is multicystic dysplastic kidney, a sporadic developmental defect.
questions.why: Multicystic dysplastic kidney comes from abnormal differentiation of the metanephros. It is usually unilateral and not inherited, and the kidney is replaced by cysts with immature ducts and sometimes cartilage. Because the other kidney works, amniotic fluid is normal and the prognosis is good. Both forms of polycystic kidney disease are bilateral, and autosomal recessive disease shows huge kidneys in infancy with Potter sequence and congenital hepatic fibrosis. Acquired cystic disease develops in adults after years of dialysis and carries a risk of renal cell carcinoma.
whyNot: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is bilateral and usually becomes evident in adulthood. A single cystic kidney with a normal partner does not fit.
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease enlarges both kidneys, causes oligohydramnios, and comes with congenital hepatic fibrosis. This infant's right kidney and amniotic fluid were normal.
Acquired cystic disease develops in scarred kidneys of adults on long-term dialysis. It does not occur in a newborn.
Correct.

questions.stem: His 39-year-old brother carries the same mutation and has mildly enlarged cystic kidneys. Which of the following extrarenal lesions is the brother most likely to have?
options: Hemangioblastoma of the cerebellum
Multiple cysts in the liver
Facial angiofibromas
Fibrosis of portal tracts in the liver
approach: Identify the syndrome: bilateral cystic kidneys in a family with dominant inheritance is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
List its extrarenal features: hepatic cysts, berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula, and hernias.
Separate it from other genetic cystic syndromes and pick its most common extrarenal lesion.
questions.why: Hepatic cysts are the most common extrarenal lesion in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, and they become more frequent with age. Polycystins are also expressed in bile duct epithelium, so cysts form there as well. Other associations include berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula, and abdominal wall hernias. Several other genetic syndromes also cause renal cysts, so the extrarenal lesion helps identify the disease.
whyNot: Cerebellar hemangioblastoma belongs to von Hippel-Lindau disease, which causes renal cysts and clear cell renal carcinoma from loss of the VHL gene on chromosome 3.
Correct.
Facial angiofibromas belong to tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 or TSC2), which causes renal cysts and angiomyolipomas.
Congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal fibrosis accompanies autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease and leads to portal hypertension in childhood.

questions.stem: On hospital day 4, he is alert and appears euvolemic. Serum sodium is 127 mEq/L (136 to 145), serum osmolality is 262 mOsm/kg H2O (275 to 295), urine osmolality is 560 mOsm/kg H2O, and urine sodium is 62 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hyponatremia?
options: Central diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic injury
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from cystic kidneys
Inappropriate ADH release after brain injury
Primary polydipsia from increased water intake
approach: Read the plasma: low sodium and low osmolality mean too much water relative to solute.
Read the urine: an osmolality of 560 means the collecting duct is reabsorbing water, so ADH is acting despite hypotonic plasma.
Euvolemia with concentrated urine after subarachnoid hemorrhage points to inappropriate ADH secretion.
questions.why: The loop of Henle uses countercurrent multiplication to build a hyperosmotic medulla, and ADH inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting duct cells so water can follow that gradient. Normally, hypotonic plasma shuts off ADH and the urine becomes dilute. Here the urine is concentrated while the plasma is dilute, so ADH is being released inappropriately. Brain injury such as subarachnoid hemorrhage is a common cause, and urine sodium stays high because the patient is euvolemic and taking in salt.
whyNot: Central diabetes insipidus removes ADH, so the urine is dilute and serum sodium rises. Urine osmolality rises after desmopressin.
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus also gives dilute urine and high or high-normal sodium, with no response to desmopressin. Cystic kidneys can impair concentration, but his urine is concentrated.
Correct.
Primary polydipsia lowers sodium, but ADH is suppressed and the urine is maximally dilute, often below 100 mOsm/kg H2O.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a mutation in the gene on chromosome 16 that is responsible for most cases of his disease. Which of the following correctly identifies the gene product and the probability that his 16-year-old daughter inherited the mutation?
options: Polycystin-1; 50 percent
Polycystin-2; 50 percent
Fibrocystin; 25 percent
Polycystin-1; 25 percent
approach: Match the chromosome to the gene: PKD1 on chromosome 16 encodes polycystin-1.
Recall the inheritance: autosomal dominant, so an affected heterozygous parent passes the mutant allele to each child half the time.
Combine the two.
questions.why: About 85 percent of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is due to PKD1 on chromosome 16, which encodes polycystin-1. Most of the rest is due to PKD2 on chromosome 4, which encodes polycystin-2 and causes a milder disease with later kidney failure. Polycystins work together in the primary cilia of tubular cells, and their loss lets cysts grow. Because inheritance is autosomal dominant, each child of an affected heterozygous parent has a 50 percent chance of inheriting the mutation.
whyNot: Correct.
Polycystin-2 is encoded by PKD2 on chromosome 4. It causes a minority of cases.
Fibrocystin is encoded by PKHD1, the gene of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. A 25 percent risk applies when both parents are carriers.
Polycystin-1 is the right protein, but 25 percent is the recurrence risk for a recessive disease. A dominant mutation passes to half of an affected parent's children.

dx: Unilateral renal agenesis with compensatory hypertrophy
case: A 27-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department after a low-speed motor vehicle collision. She has no significant injuries. Abdominal CT shows no right kidney and an enlarged left kidney measuring 13.8 cm (normal adult length about 10 to 12 cm) with normal contrast enhancement. She has no history of urinary tract disease. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), and urinalysis is normal. Cystoscopy performed later shows no right ureteral orifice and no right half of the trigone. Diagnosis: right unilateral renal agenesis with compensatory hypertrophy of the left kidney.

questions.stem: Which of the following embryonic structures normally gives rise to the organ that is missing on her right side, and when does that structure first appear?
options: Pronephros, in the fourth week
Metanephros, in the fifth week
Mesonephros, in the fourth week
Metanephros, in the tenth week
approach: Identify the missing organ: the permanent kidney.
Recall the three kidney systems in order: pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros.
Only the metanephros persists as the adult kidney, and it appears in the fifth week.
questions.why: Three kidney systems form in sequence from intermediate mesoderm. The pronephros appears early in the fourth week and is rudimentary and nonfunctional. The mesonephros forms late in the fourth week and works briefly as an interim kidney, and its duct gives rise to the ureteric bud. The metanephros appears in the fifth week and becomes the permanent kidney, starting to make urine around the end of the first trimester.
whyNot: The pronephros is a transient, nonfunctional structure that regresses. It never forms the adult kidney.
Correct.
The mesonephros functions briefly and then mostly regresses, though its duct contributes to the male genital ducts and gives rise to the ureteric bud.
The metanephros is the right structure, but it appears in the fifth week. By about the end of the first trimester it is already producing urine.

questions.stem: If her renal agenesis had been bilateral, which of the following would most likely have caused death shortly after birth?
options: Pulmonary hypoplasia
Hyperkalemic cardiac arrest
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
Intraventricular hemorrhage
approach: Identify the first consequence: with no kidneys, the fetus makes no urine, so amniotic fluid is very low.
Recall what amniotic fluid does: it is needed for lung growth and gives the fetus room to move.
Oligohydramnios causes Potter sequence, and the lethal part is underdeveloped lungs.
questions.why: From the second trimester onward, fetal urine provides most of the amniotic fluid. Without kidneys, oligohydramnios develops, and the compressed fetus forms Potter sequence: flattened facies, limb and positional deformities, and pulmonary hypoplasia. The placenta clears wastes before birth, so uremia is not the immediate threat. Newborns die of respiratory failure from small, underdeveloped lungs.
whyNot: Correct.
Without kidneys, potassium would rise over days after birth, but respiratory failure from small lungs occurs within hours.
Hypoplastic left heart is a separate cardiac malformation. It is not a consequence of absent fetal urine.
Intraventricular hemorrhage is a complication of prematurity due to a fragile germinal matrix. It does not follow from renal agenesis.

questions.stem: In her solitary kidney, each remaining nephron shows increased glomerular plasma flow and increased single-nephron GFR, while filtration fraction stays about the same. Which of the following arteriolar changes best explains these findings?
options: Constriction of the efferent arteriole
Constriction of the afferent arteriole
Dilation of the efferent arteriole
Dilation of the afferent arteriole
approach: Write down the pattern: plasma flow up, GFR up, filtration fraction unchanged.
Predict each change: afferent dilation raises both flow and glomerular pressure; efferent constriction raises GFR but lowers flow, so filtration fraction rises.
Only afferent dilation raises both by similar amounts.
questions.why: Filtration fraction is GFR divided by renal plasma flow. Dilating the afferent arteriole lets more blood into the glomerulus and transmits more pressure to its capillaries, so plasma flow and GFR both rise and filtration fraction changes little. This adaptive hyperfiltration lets one kidney do the work of two. Over decades, the higher glomerular pressure may contribute to proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis in some people with a single kidney.
whyNot: Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure and GFR but reduces plasma flow, so filtration fraction rises. This is the angiotensin II effect.
Afferent constriction lowers both plasma flow and GFR, as with NSAIDs blocking vasodilating prostaglandins or in sympathetic activation.
Efferent dilation raises plasma flow but lowers glomerular pressure and GFR, so filtration fraction falls. This is the effect of ACE inhibitors.
Correct.

topics: Arteriolar control of GFR and RPF

questions.stem: Which of the following developmental failures best accounts for her absent right kidney, ureteral orifice, and hemitrigone?
options: Failure of the right kidney to ascend from the pelvis
Failure of metanephric mesenchyme to form nephrons
Absence of the right ureteric bud
Fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys
approach: Note what is missing: kidney, ureter, ureteral orifice, and half of the trigone.
Recall what each tissue builds: the ureteric bud forms the ureter, pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts; the metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons, but only when the bud induces it.
Missing ureter structures plus missing kidney means the bud never formed, so induction never happened.
questions.why: The kidney forms by reciprocal induction. The metanephric mesenchyme signals the ureteric bud to grow and branch into the ureter, pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts. The bud in turn induces the mesenchyme to form nephrons from Bowman capsule to the distal convoluted tubule. With no bud, there is no ureter, no ureteral orifice, and no ipsilateral trigone, and the mesenchyme is never induced, so no kidney forms.
whyNot: Failed ascent produces a pelvic kidney, which is present and has a ureter. Her kidney is absent altogether.
If the bud formed but the mesenchyme failed to respond, a ureter and ureteral orifice would still be present, sometimes ending blindly. She has neither.
Correct.
Fusion of the lower poles produces a horseshoe kidney trapped below the inferior mesenteric artery. Both kidneys and both ureters are present.

dx: Duplex collecting system with vesicoureteral reflux and acute pyelonephritis in a toddler
case: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of fever, vomiting, and irritability for 2 days. Temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 94/56 mm Hg. She cries when pressure is applied at the left costovertebral angle. Urinalysis of a catheterized specimen shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite, numerous neutrophils, and white blood cell casts. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of Escherichia coli. Ultrasonography shows a left kidney with two separate collecting systems. Voiding cystourethrography shows reflux into the ureter draining the left lower pole, which enters the bladder separately from the upper pole ureter. Diagnosis: complete left duplex collecting system with vesicoureteral reflux and acute pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: Ultrasonography also shows that the upper pole collecting system and its ureter are dilated, with the ureter ending in a cystic bulge within the bladder near the bladder neck. Which of the following best explains why the upper pole moiety is obstructed while the lower pole moiety refluxes?
options: Upper pole ureter has a short tunnel that opens laterally
Upper pole ureter lacks a muscular coat along its length
Upper pole ureter opens caudal and medial to the other
Upper pole ureter is compressed by an aberrant lower pole artery
approach: Recall the rule for complete duplication: the two ureters cross so that the upper pole ureter inserts lower and more medially, and the lower pole ureter inserts higher and more laterally.
Relate position to function: a low, medial, ectopic orifice often has a ureterocele and obstructs; a high, lateral orifice has a short tunnel and refluxes.
Match to her findings: upper pole dilated with a ureterocele, lower pole refluxing.
questions.why: In a complete duplex system, the upper pole ureter enters the bladder caudal and medial to the lower pole ureter. This is the Weigert-Meyer rule. The ectopic upper pole orifice may sit near the bladder neck, often with a ureterocele, and it tends to obstruct. In girls it can even open below the urethral sphincter and cause constant dribbling. The lower pole ureter opens cranial and lateral with a short intravesical tunnel, so it tends to reflux, as in this patient.
whyNot: A lateral orifice with a short tunnel describes the lower pole ureter, which refluxes. It does not explain obstruction of the upper pole.
Absent or abnormal muscle in the distal ureter is a cause of primary megaureter. It does not explain the paired pattern of an obstructed upper pole and a refluxing lower pole.
Correct.
A lower pole crossing vessel can kink the ureteropelvic junction and cause obstruction there. The obstruction here is at a ureterocele inside the bladder.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the organism most likely reached her kidney?
options: Hematogenous seeding during transient bacteremia
Lymphatic spread from the adjacent colon
Direct extension from a perinephric abscess
Ascent from the bladder up the ureter
approach: Identify the organism and its source: E. coli from fecal flora that colonizes the periurethral area.
Identify the anatomic setup: reflux carries bladder urine up to the renal pelvis.
Most acute pyelonephritis is ascending, and reflux makes ascent easy.
questions.why: Most acute pyelonephritis is an ascending infection. E. coli from the bowel colonizes the periurethral area, enters the bladder through the short female urethra, and reflux carries infected urine to the renal pelvis and into the collecting ducts. Neutrophils then fill the interstitium and tubules, and white blood cell casts form inside the tubules, which proves the kidney is involved. Clinically this produces fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness.
whyNot: Hematogenous pyelonephritis is uncommon and is usually due to Staphylococcus aureus or Candida during sepsis or endocarditis. E. coli with reflux points to ascent.
Lymphatic spread from the bowel is not a recognized main route to the kidney. Enteric organisms reach the kidney by ascending the urinary tract.
A perinephric abscess is a complication of pyelonephritis that spreads outward from the kidney. It is not the source.
Correct.

questions.stem: If the reflux persists with repeated infections, coarse scars are most likely to form at the upper and lower poles of the kidney. Which of the following best explains this distribution?
options: Compound papillae at the poles have widely open duct orifices
The poles receive the least blood flow from segmental arteries
Calyces at the poles empty more slowly into the renal pelvis
Cortex at the poles has the highest density of nephrons
approach: Recall how reflux injures the kidney: infected urine must enter the collecting ducts, which is called intrarenal reflux.
Recall papilla shape: simple papillae have slit-like openings that close under pressure; compound papillae, found mainly at the poles, have round openings that stay open.
Scars form where intrarenal reflux occurs, so they cluster at the poles.
questions.why: Reflux damages the kidney when infected urine enters the collecting ducts through the papillae. Simple papillae are cone-shaped with slit-like duct openings that close when pelvic pressure rises. Compound papillae, made of fused papillae and concentrated at the upper and lower poles, are flat or concave with round, gaping openings that allow urine to flow back into the ducts. That is why reflux nephropathy produces coarse polar scars over blunted, dilated calyces.
whyNot: Correct.
Polar regions are supplied by their own segmental arteries and are not relatively ischemic. Uneven blood flow does not explain where reflux scars form.
Calyceal emptying is not slower at the poles. The key factor is whether the papilla lets urine back into the collecting ducts.
Nephron density is not highest at the poles, and nephron number would not decide where refluxed urine enters.

questions.stem: Despite intravenous antibiotics, she remains febrile on hospital day 5. Ultrasonography shows a fluid collection in the perirenal fat around the lower pole of the left kidney. Along which of the following paths is this collection most likely to spread?
options: Through the parietal peritoneum into the greater sac
Inferiorly within the renal fascia toward the pelvis
Laterally through the abdominal wall into the flank
Anteriorly through the renal fascia into the lesser sac
approach: Identify the space: a perinephric abscess lies in the perirenal fat inside the renal fascia, behind the peritoneum.
Recall how the renal fascia is closed: its layers are fused above and laterally but only loosely joined below.
Fluid follows the path of least resistance, which is downward toward the pelvis.
questions.why: The kidney sits in the retroperitoneum inside perirenal fat, which is enclosed by the renal fascia. The anterior and posterior layers of this fascia are fused above the suprarenal gland and along the lateral border, but they are loosely joined below. A perinephric abscess is therefore contained in the retroperitoneum and tends to track inferiorly toward the pelvis. The same posterior position of the kidney, against the 12th rib and posterior abdominal wall, is why pressure at the costovertebral angle hurts in pyelonephritis.
whyNot: The kidney and its fat are retroperitoneal and enclosed by renal fascia, so spread into the peritoneal cavity is uncommon.
Correct.
The fascial layers are fused along the lateral border, which blocks lateral spread. Pus would have to break through fascia and muscle to reach the flank.
The anterior layer of renal fascia and the parietal peritoneum separate the kidney from the lesser sac. Spread there is not the usual path.

dx: Hemolytic uremic syndrome after Escherichia coli O157:H7 diarrhea
case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of pallor and decreased urine output for 1 day. Seven days ago, 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger, he developed abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhea, which have since resolved. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 112/72 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL (11.5 to 13.5), and platelet count is 38,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Serum creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7). Stool culture grows sorbitol-nonfermenting Escherichia coli O157:H7. Diagnosis: hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy shows fibrin-platelet thrombi in glomerular capillaries and in the arterioles that supply them. These arterioles branch directly from which of the following vessels?
options: Cortical radiate arteries within the cortex
Arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction
Interlobar arteries between the renal pyramids
Segmental arteries within the renal sinus
approach: Name the arterioles that supply glomeruli: afferent arterioles.
Trace the arterial tree: renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate, cortical radiate, then afferent arterioles.
Afferent arterioles come straight off the cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries.
questions.why: Blood runs from the renal artery to segmental arteries in the sinus, interlobar arteries between the pyramids, and arcuate arteries along the corticomedullary junction. Cortical radiate arteries rise from the arcuate arteries into the cortex and give off afferent arterioles, each feeding one glomerulus. The efferent arteriole then forms peritubular capillaries or, near the medulla, the vasa recta. Thrombi in afferent arterioles and glomeruli cut off flow to the tubules downstream, which is why HUS causes acute kidney injury.
whyNot: Correct.
Arcuate arteries run along the base of the pyramids and give off the cortical radiate arteries, not afferent arterioles.
Interlobar arteries run between the pyramids toward the cortex and branch into arcuate arteries.
Segmental arteries lie in the renal sinus and give rise to interlobar arteries. They are several branchings away from the glomeruli.

questions.stem: The toxin made by this organism enters endothelial cells after binding a glycolipid receptor on their surface. Which of the following is its intracellular action?
options: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2
Removal of an adenine from 28S ribosomal RNA
ADP-ribosylation of the Gs alpha subunit
Activation of guanylate cyclase in enterocytes
approach: Identify the toxin: E. coli O157:H7 makes Shiga toxin.
Recall its structure: the B subunit binds the glycolipid Gb3 on endothelium, and the A subunit enters the cell.
Recall what the A subunit does: it cuts an adenine from 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit, stopping protein synthesis.
questions.why: Shiga toxin has one A subunit and five B subunits. The B subunits bind globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), which is plentiful on glomerular endothelium, and the A subunit removes an adenine from 28S rRNA in the 60S ribosomal subunit. Protein synthesis stops and endothelial cells are injured, so platelets and fibrin deposit in small vessels. The thrombi consume platelets and shear red cells into schistocytes, giving the triad of thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and acute kidney injury. TTP produces a similar microangiopathy from ADAMTS13 deficiency, which leaves unusually large von Willebrand factor multimers in the blood.
whyNot: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 is the action of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A. It also stops protein synthesis, by a different target.
Correct.
ADP-ribosylation of Gs keeps adenylate cyclase on. Cholera toxin and the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli act this way and cause watery diarrhea.
Activation of guanylate cyclase is the action of the heat-stable toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli, which causes watery diarrhea without endothelial injury.

questions.stem: Urine studies show sodium 64 mEq/L and creatinine 40 mg/dL. Serum sodium is 134 mEq/L (135 to 145). Which of the following best classifies his acute kidney injury?
options: Prerenal injury; FENa about 0.3 percent
Prerenal injury; FENa about 3 percent
Intrinsic injury; FENa about 0.3 percent
Intrinsic injury; FENa about 3 percent
approach: Use FENa = (urine Na x plasma creatinine) / (plasma Na x urine creatinine) x 100.
Calculate: (64 x 2.6) / (134 x 40) x 100 = 166 / 5,360 x 100, which is about 3 percent.
A FENa above 2 percent means the tubules are failing to reabsorb sodium, which indicates intrinsic injury.
questions.why: Fractional excretion of sodium compares the sodium the kidney excretes with the sodium it filters. In prerenal injury, the tubules are intact and hold on to sodium, so FENa is below 1 percent. When tubules are damaged, as when ischemia downstream of thrombosed glomeruli injures them, sodium is lost and FENa rises above 2 percent. His value of about 3 percent fits intrinsic injury from the thrombotic microangiopathy, even though his earlier diarrhea could have caused a prerenal component.
whyNot: A FENa of 0.3 percent would fit prerenal injury, but his calculated value is about ten times higher.
A FENa of about 3 percent does not fit prerenal injury, because intact tubules would conserve sodium and keep it below 1 percent.
Intrinsic injury is the right category, but 0.3 percent comes from a calculation error. His FENa is about 3 percent.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two years later, his 7-year-old sister has fever, left flank pain, and white blood cell casts in her urine. Culture grows an Escherichia coli strain that does not produce Shiga toxin. Which of the following virulence factors most likely allowed this strain to colonize her upper urinary tract?
options: Type 1 fimbriae binding mannosylated uroplakin
Heat-stable toxin activating guanylate cyclase
P fimbriae binding Gal-Gal on uroepithelium
Intimin binding enterocyte Tir receptors
approach: Identify the infection: fever, flank pain, and white blood cell casts mean acute pyelonephritis.
Recall the adhesins of uropathogenic E. coli: type 1 fimbriae for the bladder, P fimbriae for the upper tract.
Pick the adhesin linked to pyelonephritis.
questions.why: Uropathogenic E. coli comes from fecal flora and is the most common cause of urinary tract infection. Type 1 fimbriae bind mannose residues on bladder uroplakins and are mainly linked to cystitis. P fimbriae bind galactose-galactose (Gal-Gal) residues on glycolipids of the upper urinary tract and kidney, which lets the bacteria hold on against urine flow. P fimbriae are strongly associated with pyelonephritis.
whyNot: Type 1 fimbriae bind mannose on bladder uroplakins and are associated mostly with cystitis.
Heat-stable toxin belongs to enterotoxigenic E. coli and causes watery traveler's diarrhea. It plays no part in urinary infection.
Correct.
Intimin binds Tir on enterocytes to form attaching and effacing lesions in enteropathogenic and enterohemorrhagic E. coli. It is an intestinal adhesin.

case: A 39-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a severe headache and blurred vision for 2 days. Three years ago, he was told that he had high blood pressure but did not begin treatment. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 238/136 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows papilledema, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots. Serum creatinine is 3.8 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3); it was 1.0 mg/dL 1 year ago. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and a blood smear shows schistocytes. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and red blood cells. Plasma renin activity is markedly increased. Diagnosis: malignant hypertension with malignant nephrosclerosis.

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy is performed. Which of the following arteriolar findings is most likely?
options: Homogeneous pink hyaline thickening of the wall
Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells
Medial calcification without luminal narrowing
Concentric smooth muscle layering with fibrinoid necrosis
approach: Separate the two forms of hypertensive kidney disease: benign (slow, long-standing) and malignant (abrupt, severe).
Recall the arteriolar lesion of each: hyaline arteriolosclerosis in benign; hyperplastic onion-skin arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis in malignant.
His pressure, papilledema, rapid creatinine rise, and schistocytes mark malignant hypertension.
questions.why: In malignant hypertension, very high pressure injures arteriolar endothelium. Smooth muscle cells proliferate in concentric layers with reduplicated basement membrane, giving an onion-skin appearance, and the wall can undergo fibrinoid necrosis. The narrowed lumens cause ischemia, which drives renin release and raises pressure further. The kidney surface shows pinpoint hemorrhages (the flea-bitten kidney), and acute renal failure follows.
whyNot: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the lesion of benign nephrosclerosis and of diabetes. It gives symmetrically shrunken kidneys with finely granular surfaces over years.
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells describes giant cell or Takayasu arteritis. These affect larger arteries, not renal arterioles.
Medial calcification without narrowing is Monckeberg sclerosis of muscular arteries. It is usually clinically silent.
Correct.

questions.stem: In healthy kidneys, a rise in mean arterial pressure from 90 to 140 mm Hg causes little change in GFR. His blood pressure exceeded the upper limit of this protection. Which of the following normally keeps a rise in arterial pressure from reaching the glomerular capillaries?
options: Efferent arteriolar constriction caused by angiotensin II
Afferent arteriolar dilation signaled by the macula densa
Afferent arteriolar constriction in response to wall stretch
Mesangial cell contraction in response to natriuretic peptide
approach: To protect the glomerulus from a pressure rise, the vessel upstream of it must narrow.
Recall the two autoregulatory mechanisms: the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback. Both constrict the afferent arteriole.
Choose the option that constricts the afferent arteriole: the myogenic response to stretch.
questions.why: Autoregulation keeps renal blood flow and GFR nearly constant over a mean arterial pressure of about 75 to 160 mm Hg. In the myogenic response, higher pressure stretches the afferent arteriole, stretch-activated channels depolarize its smooth muscle, calcium enters, and the vessel constricts. Tubuloglomerular feedback adds to this, because more filtered sodium chloride reaching the macula densa triggers afferent constriction through adenosine. Above the upper limit, as in this patient, pressure reaches the arterioles and glomeruli and damages them.
whyNot: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole when pressure falls, which keeps GFR up. Efferent constriction would raise glomerular pressure further when arterial pressure rises.
When pressure and filtration rise, the macula densa senses more sodium chloride and signals afferent constriction. Dilation would let even more pressure through.
Correct.
Natriuretic peptides relax mesangial cells and dilate the afferent arteriole, which increases GFR. They do not protect the glomerulus from high pressure.

questions.stem: Before this presentation, his physician had considered screening him for primary hyperaldosteronism. Which of the following sets of findings would most strongly have supported that diagnosis?
options: High renin, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis
Low renin, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis
Low renin, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis
High renin, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis
approach: Start with aldosterone's actions in the collecting duct: sodium reabsorption with potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.
Predict the electrolytes: hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.
Predict renin: the extra sodium and volume raise pressure, which suppresses renin from the juxtaglomerular cells.
questions.why: An aldosterone-producing adenoma or adrenal hyperplasia makes aldosterone without renin. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption through ENaC and drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, causing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. The added sodium raises blood pressure, and pressure natriuresis then increases sodium excretion until intake and output balance again. This escape limits edema but leaves the pressure high, and the expanded volume suppresses renin. Malignant hypertension, as in this patient now, has high renin and secondary hyperaldosteronism.
whyNot: High renin with hypokalemia and alkalosis is secondary hyperaldosteronism, as in renovascular or malignant hypertension. It is the pattern expected with his high renin, not the primary adrenal disorder.
Correct.
Low renin with hyperkalemia and acidosis is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (type 4 renal tubular acidosis), common in diabetic kidney disease.
High renin with hyperkalemia and acidosis fits primary adrenal insufficiency, where the adrenal cannot make aldosterone despite high renin.

questions.stem: His markedly increased plasma renin activity reflects ischemia from narrowed renal arterioles. Which of the following cells sense the reduced perfusion pressure and secrete renin?
options: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
Macula densa cells of the thick ascending limb
Extraglomerular mesangial cells near the vascular pole
Intraglomerular mesangial cells between capillary loops
approach: List the parts of the juxtaglomerular apparatus: juxtaglomerular cells, macula densa, and extraglomerular mesangial cells.
Assign the jobs: juxtaglomerular cells sense stretch and secrete renin; the macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride.
Low perfusion pressure is sensed in the arteriolar wall, so the answer is the juxtaglomerular cells.
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that contain renin granules. They act as baroreceptors, releasing renin when stretch of the arteriole falls, and they also respond to sympathetic beta-1 stimulation and macula densa signals. In malignant nephrosclerosis, narrowed arterioles lower the pressure the juxtaglomerular cells sense, so renin rises and drives the pressure even higher.
whyNot: Correct.
Macula densa cells sit in the distal thick ascending limb and sense tubular sodium chloride. They signal the juxtaglomerular cells but do not secrete renin.
Extraglomerular (lacis) mesangial cells lie between the arterioles and the macula densa and likely relay signals between them. They do not store renin.
Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the capillary loops, contract, and phagocytose trapped proteins. They are not the main source of renin.

dx: Fibromuscular dysplasia with renal artery stenosis
case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up of high blood pressure first noted 4 months ago. She takes no medications and has no family history of hypertension. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 174/106 mm Hg. An epigastric bruit with systolic and diastolic components is heard. Serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), bicarbonate is 30 mEq/L (22 to 28), and creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are both increased. CT angiography shows alternating narrowing and dilation of the middle and distal right main renal artery. The right kidney measures 9.0 cm, and the left kidney measures 11.5 cm. Diagnosis: fibromuscular dysplasia with right renal artery stenosis.

questions.stem: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is started. Two weeks later, renal scintigraphy shows a sharp fall in the GFR of the right kidney. Which of the following changes in the right kidney best explains this?
options: Afferent constriction, lowering renal plasma flow
Efferent dilation, lowering glomerular pressure
Efferent constriction, raising filtration fraction
Afferent dilation, raising glomerular pressure
approach: Recognize the setting: low perfusion pressure beyond the stenosis.
Recall how the kidney protects GFR there: angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and keeps glomerular pressure up.
Predict the drug effect: removing angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole, glomerular pressure drops, and GFR falls.
questions.why: Beyond a stenosis, pressure in the afferent arteriole is low. Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent one, which raises glomerular capillary pressure and keeps GFR up while plasma flow falls, so filtration fraction rises. An ACE inhibitor removes this support, so the efferent arteriole dilates, glomerular pressure falls, and GFR in the affected kidney drops. This is the basis of the fall in GFR seen with ACE inhibitors in renal artery stenosis.
whyNot: ACE inhibitors do not constrict the afferent arteriole. Afferent constriction is caused by NSAIDs, sympathetic activity, or the myogenic response.
Correct.
Efferent constriction is what angiotensin II does. The drug removes this effect, so GFR falls.
Afferent dilation would raise glomerular pressure and GFR, the opposite of what happened.

topics: Angiotensin II and the efferent arteriole

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic changes most likely underlies the angiographic appearance of her renal artery?
options: Medial fibroplasia alternating with thinned arterial wall
Lipid-rich intimal plaque at the arterial ostium
Granulomatous panarteritis with multinucleated giant cells
Concentric medial calcification without stenosis
approach: Read the clues: a young woman, a beaded middle to distal renal artery, and renin-driven hypertension.
Separate the two main causes of renal artery stenosis: atherosclerosis at the ostium in older adults, and fibromuscular dysplasia farther along the artery in young women.
Recall the histology of the common form of fibromuscular dysplasia: ridges of thickened fibromuscular media alternate with thin, dilated segments.
questions.why: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic disease of medium arteries, most often the renal and carotid arteries of young to middle-aged women. In the most common form, medial fibroplasia, thickened ridges of fibrous tissue and smooth muscle alternate with thinned segments that bulge outward, giving a string-of-beads appearance in the middle and distal renal artery. The stenosis lowers pressure at the juxtaglomerular cells, renin rises, and secondary hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemia. The underperfused kidney gradually shrinks, and turbulent flow produces a bruit.
whyNot: Correct.
An ostial lipid plaque is atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis, seen in older adults with vascular risk factors. It narrows the origin of the artery without beading.
Granulomatous panarteritis with giant cells is Takayasu or giant cell arteritis. It causes long, smooth narrowing and systemic inflammation rather than beading.
Medial calcification without stenosis is Monckeberg sclerosis. It does not narrow the lumen or cause hypertension.

questions.stem: Reduced flow through her right renal artery lowers perfusion of the renal medulla as well as the cortex. Most blood reaching the medulla arrives through which of the following vessels?
options: Peritubular capillaries of superficial cortical nephrons
Afferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons
Vasa recta from juxtamedullary efferent arterioles
Arcuate arteries entering the renal pyramids directly
approach: Recall that most medullary blood has already passed through a glomerulus.
Identify which glomeruli lie next to the medulla: those of juxtamedullary nephrons.
Their efferent arterioles descend as the vasa recta, which supply the medulla.
questions.why: The medulla receives blood mainly from the efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary glomeruli. These efferent arterioles dip into the medulla as long, hairpin vessels called the vasa recta, which run beside the loops of Henle and then drain back to arcuate and interlobar veins. Because this blood has already passed through two capillary beds and flows slowly, medullary oxygen tension is low. That slow countercurrent flow also helps preserve the concentration gradient.
whyNot: Efferent arterioles of superficial cortical nephrons form peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules. They do not supply the medulla.
Afferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons feed their glomeruli. The blood reaches the medulla only after leaving the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole.
Correct.
Arcuate arteries run along the corticomedullary junction and give off cortical radiate arteries. The medulla is supplied mainly after blood passes through juxtamedullary glomeruli.

questions.stem: Her hypokalemia results from secondary hyperaldosteronism. Which of the following best describes how aldosterone acts on its target cells in the collecting duct?
options: Binds a V2 receptor and inserts aquaporin-2 channels
Binds a membrane receptor and increases distal calcium reabsorption
Binds a cytosolic receptor that increases NKCC2 synthesis
Binds a cytosolic receptor that increases ENaC synthesis
approach: Identify the hormone type: aldosterone is a steroid, so it acts through an intracellular receptor that changes gene expression.
Identify the target: principal cells of the collecting duct.
Recall the products: more apical ENaC channels and more basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, which drive sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.
questions.why: Aldosterone is a steroid that enters principal cells and binds the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor. The complex moves to the nucleus and increases synthesis of apical ENaC channels and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pumps. More sodium is reabsorbed, the lumen becomes more negative, and more potassium is secreted through apical channels. In renal artery stenosis, high renin drives this process, which explains her hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.
whyNot: ADH binds the V2 receptor, a membrane receptor that raises cAMP and inserts aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. That changes water reabsorption, not potassium secretion.
PTH acts on a membrane receptor in the distal convoluted tubule to increase calcium reabsorption. It is a peptide hormone with a different target.
NKCC2 is the cotransporter of the thick ascending limb, which loop diuretics block. Aldosterone's main sodium effect is on ENaC in the collecting duct.
Correct.

topics: Hormones acting on the distal nephron

dx: Embolic renal infarction from atrial fibrillation
case: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe, constant left flank pain with nausea. He has atrial fibrillation and stopped taking warfarin 2 months ago. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 118/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood with 10 to 20 RBC/hpf and no crystals. Serum lactate dehydrogenase is 920 U/L (100 to 250), and serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Contrast-enhanced CT shows a wedge-shaped, nonenhancing region in the upper pole of the left kidney, with its broad base at the capsule. Diagnosis: embolic renal infarction due to atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the shape of the affected region?
options: Venous outflow from the upper pole is obstructed
Cortical capillaries have the lowest oxygen tension
Interlobar arteries lack functional anastomoses
Collateral flow from capsular arteries spares the medulla
approach: Describe the lesion: a wedge with its apex toward the hilum and its base at the capsule.
Recall the arterial pattern: segmental and interlobar arteries branch outward like a tree and do not connect with their neighbors.
Block one branch and the whole fan-shaped territory it supplies dies, giving a wedge.
questions.why: The segmental and interlobar arteries of the kidney are end arteries, with no meaningful anastomoses between neighboring branches. Each artery supplies a territory that widens as it branches toward the cortex. When an embolus blocks one, the whole territory dies, producing a wedge with its apex at the occlusion and its base at the capsule. A thin rim of outer cortex can survive on capsular collaterals.
whyNot: Venous occlusion, as in renal vein thrombosis, causes a swollen, congested kidney. It does not produce a sharply wedge-shaped arterial infarct.
Oxygen tension is lowest in the medulla, not the cortex. Low oxygen tension would not explain a wedge-shaped zone.
Correct.
Capsular collaterals preserve a thin rim of outer cortex, not the medulla. The medulla lies inside the infarct, toward its apex.

questions.stem: The upper pole of his left kidney lies at about the level of the T11 to T12 vertebrae. Which of the following structures lies directly posterior to this part of the kidney?
options: Psoas major muscle
Quadratus lumborum muscle
Transversus abdominis aponeurosis
Diaphragm
approach: Place the kidney: retroperitoneal, from about T12 to L3, with the left slightly higher than the right.
Recall the posterior relations from top to bottom: diaphragm and lower ribs above; psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis below.
The upper pole rests on the diaphragm, with the pleural recess behind it.
questions.why: The kidneys lie in the retroperitoneum from about T12 to L3. The right kidney sits a little lower because the liver lies above it, so the left upper pole reaches about the 11th rib. Behind the upper pole lies the diaphragm, which separates it from the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura and the lower ribs. Lower down, the kidney rests on the psoas major medially, the quadratus lumborum, and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis laterally.
whyNot: The psoas major lies behind the medial part of the lower kidney. It is too low and too medial to sit behind the upper pole.
The quadratus lumborum lies behind the middle and lower parts of the kidney, below the diaphragm.
The transversus abdominis aponeurosis lies behind the lateral border of the lower kidney.
Correct.

questions.stem: If the infarcted tissue were examined 3 days after the event, which of the following findings would most likely be seen?
options: Pale coagulative necrosis with ghost cell outlines
Red hemorrhagic necrosis from dual blood supply
Liquefactive necrosis forming a fluid-filled cavity in the cortex
Caseous necrosis with surrounding granulomas
approach: Identify the tissue and the cause: a solid organ with end arteries, blocked by an embolus.
Recall the infarct type: arterial occlusion in a solid organ gives a pale (white) infarct.
Recall the necrosis pattern for ischemia outside the brain: coagulative, with cell outlines preserved for days.
questions.why: Arterial occlusion in a solid organ with end arteries, such as the kidney, heart, or spleen, produces a pale infarct because little blood seeps into the dead tissue. Ischemia denatures structural proteins and enzymes, so the cells die but keep their outlines as ghost cells for several days. A rim of hyperemia and inflammation forms at the edge of the wedge. Over weeks the area is replaced by a depressed fibrous scar.
whyNot: Correct.
Red infarcts occur in tissues with a dual blood supply or loose structure, such as the lung and small bowel, or after venous occlusion or reperfusion. The kidney has end arteries.
Liquefactive necrosis is the pattern of ischemia in the brain and of abscesses. Ischemic kidney tissue undergoes coagulative necrosis.
Caseous necrosis with granulomas is the pattern of tuberculosis and some fungal infections. It is not caused by ischemia.

questions.stem: Three months later, his serum creatinine is stable at 1.5 mg/dL. A 24-hour urine collection has a volume of 1,440 mL and a creatinine concentration of 90 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes his creatinine clearance and its relation to his true GFR?
options: About 60 mL/min, slightly below true GFR
About 60 mL/min, slightly above true GFR
About 90 mL/min, slightly above true GFR
About 135 mL/min, slightly above true GFR
approach: Convert urine flow: 1,440 mL over 1,440 minutes is 1.0 mL/min.
Apply clearance = (U x V) / P: (90 mg/dL x 1.0 mL/min) / 1.5 mg/dL = 60 mL/min.
Recall that creatinine is filtered and also slightly secreted, so its clearance runs a little above the true GFR.
questions.why: Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of a substance each minute, equal to urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration. Here that is 90 x 1.0 / 1.5, or 60 mL/min. Inulin is filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR exactly. Creatinine is filtered and also secreted in small amounts by the proximal tubule, so creatinine clearance overestimates GFR by roughly 10 to 20 percent, more so as kidney function falls.
whyNot: The value is right, but creatinine secretion makes its clearance higher than GFR, not lower. A clearance below GFR means net reabsorption, as with urea.
Correct.
90 mL/min comes from multiplying urine concentration by urine flow without dividing by plasma creatinine.
135 mL/min comes from multiplying by plasma creatinine instead of dividing by it.
